items.title: Top k words with Counter
items.prompt: Write `top_k(words, k)` returning the `k` most common words, most common first.
hints: collections has a dict subclass made for counting.
Counter(words).most_common(k) returns [(word, count), ...] sorted by count.
return [w for w, _ in Counter(words).most_common(k)]  (after from collections import Counter)
items.lesson: `Counter(iterable)` counts in one call; `.most_common(k)` gives the top k pairs. Missing keys read as 0, and Counters support `+`, `-`, `&`, `|`.
items.ts: const c = new Map(); for (const w of words) c.set(w, (c.get(w) ?? 0) + 1); [...c].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, k)

items.title: Group by first letter
items.prompt: Write `group_by_initial(words)` returning a dict letter → list of words (in input order).
hints: A dict whose missing keys start as an empty list would make this a two-liner.
defaultdict(list) calls list() for a missing key, so you can .append right away.
groups = defaultdict(list); for w in words: groups[w[0]].append(w); return groups
items.lesson: `defaultdict(factory)` calls the factory for missing keys: `list` for grouping, `int` for counting, `set` for unique members.
items.ts: (groups[w[0]] ??= []).push(w)

items.title: Keep the last n items
items.prompt: Write `last_n(iterable, n)` returning a list of the final `n` items. Must work on huge iterables without storing them all.
hints: A double-ended queue can be bounded: old items fall off the other end.
deque(iterable, maxlen=n) keeps only the last n items.
return list(deque(iterable, maxlen=n))
items.lesson: `deque` has O(1) `append`/`appendleft`/`pop`/`popleft` (a list's `pop(0)` is O(n)). `maxlen=` makes it a ring buffer.
items.ts: // no built-in deque in JS; arr.slice(-n) needs the whole array in memory

items.title: Recent request counter
items.prompt: Write `class RecentCounter` with `ping(t)` (t in ms, always increasing) returning how many pings happened in `[t - 3000, t]`.
items.tests:
def test_sequence():
    rc = RecentCounter()
    got = [rc.ping(t) for t in (1, 100, 3001, 3002)]
    assert got == [1, 2, 3, 3], f"got {got}"
def test_separate_instances():
    a, b = RecentCounter(), RecentCounter()
    a.ping(1)
    assert b.ping(2) == 1, "each counter keeps its own queue"
hints: Store the ping times in a queue created in __init__; drop old ones from the front.
self.q = deque(); in ping: append t, then while self.q[0] < t - 3000: popleft().
self.q.append(t); while self.q[0] < t - 3000: self.q.popleft(); return len(self.q)
items.lesson: Use `deque` whenever you take from the front (queues, BFS, sliding windows): `popleft()` is O(1).
items.ts: class RecentCounter { q: number[] = []; ping(t: number) { ... } }

items.title: LRU cache
items.prompt: Write `LRUCache(capacity)` with `get(key)` (→ value or -1) and `put(key, value)`. Over capacity, evict the least recently used key.
items.tests:
def test_evicts_lru():
    c = LRUCache(2)
    c.put(1, "a"); c.put(2, "b")
    assert c.get(1) == "a", "1 was just put"
    c.put(3, "c")  # evicts 2 (1 was used more recently)
    assert c.get(2) == -1, "2 should have been evicted"
    assert c.get(3) == "c" and c.get(1) == "a", "1 and 3 remain"
def test_update_refreshes():
    c = LRUCache(2)
    c.put(1, "a"); c.put(2, "b"); c.put(1, "A")
    c.put(3, "c")  # evicts 2
    assert c.get(1) == "A" and c.get(2) == -1, "updating 1 makes it recent"
hints: OrderedDict remembers order and can move a key to one end in O(1).
On get/put: self.d.move_to_end(key). When too big: self.d.popitem(last=False) removes the oldest.
put: self.d[key] = value; self.d.move_to_end(key); if len(self.d) > self.cap: self.d.popitem(last=False)
items.lesson: `OrderedDict.move_to_end(k)` marks k as newest; `popitem(last=False)` pops the oldest (FIFO). Both O(1). (Or just use `functools.lru_cache` for functions.)
items.ts: Map keeps insertion order: map.delete(k); map.set(k, v); map.delete(map.keys().next().value)

items.title: Kth largest with a min-heap
items.prompt: Write `kth_largest(nums, k)` using `heapq` and a heap of size k (no full sort).
hints: heapq is a MIN-heap on a plain list: h[0] is the smallest.
Push each number; whenever len(h) > k, heappop removes the smallest. The k largest remain.
for n in nums: heapq.heappush(h, n); if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)  …  return h[0]
items.lesson: `heapq` functions work on a list you own: `heappush`, `heappop`, `heapify` (O(n)). `h[0]` is the min. For a max-heap push `-x`.
items.ts: // no built-in heap in JS/TS — you'd write a PriorityQueue class

items.title: Top scorers
items.prompt: `players` is a list of `(name, score)` tuples. Write `top_scorers(players, n)` returning the names of the n highest scores, best first.
hints: heapq has a one-liner for 'the n biggest' that accepts key=.
heapq.nlargest(n, players, key=lambda p: p[1]) returns the tuples.
return [name for name, _ in heapq.nlargest(n, players, key=lambda p: p[1])]
items.lesson: `heapq.nlargest(n, xs, key=)` / `nsmallest` are O(len · log n) — better than sorting when n is small.
items.ts: [...players].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, n).map(p => p[0])

items.title: Process by priority
items.prompt: `tasks` is a list of `(priority, name)`; lower priority runs first. Write `run_order(tasks)` returning names in run order using `heapify`/`heappop`.
items.tests:
def test_basic():
    got = run_order([(3, "deploy"), (1, "test"), (2, "build")])
    assert got == ["test", "build", "deploy"], f"got {got!r}"
def test_no_mutation():
    t = [(2, "b"), (1, "a")]
    run_order(t)
    assert t == [(2, "b"), (1, "a")], "copy the list before heapify (it works in place)"
hints: Tuples compare element by element, so a heap of (priority, name) orders by priority.
h = list(tasks); heapq.heapify(h); then pop until empty.
return [heapq.heappop(h)[1] for _ in range(len(h))]
items.solution:
import heapq

def run_order(tasks):
    h = list(tasks)
    heapq.heapify(h)
    return [heapq.heappop(h)[1] for _ in range(len(h))]
items.lesson: Heap entries are often tuples `(priority, tiebreak, item)` — the tiebreak (a counter) avoids comparing items that can't be compared.
items.ts: tasks.slice().sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]).map(t => t[1])

items.title: Run-length encode
items.prompt: Write `rle(s)`: `'aaabbc'` → `'a3b2c1'`, using `itertools.groupby`.
hints: groupby(s) yields (key, group_iterator) for each run of equal consecutive items.
The group is an iterator — use len(list(g)) or sum(1 for _ in g) to count it.
return "".join(f"{ch}{len(list(g))}" for ch, g in groupby(s))
items.lesson: `groupby` only groups ADJACENT equal items — sort by the same key first if you want SQL-style grouping.
items.ts: s.match(/(.)\1*/g)?.map(r => r[0] + r.length).join('') ?? ''

items.title: Chain iterables
items.prompt: Write `merge_all(lists)` returning one list with every item from each inner iterable, in order, using `itertools`.
hints: itertools.chain(a, b, c) iterates a, then b, then c.
You have a list OF iterables, so use the alternate constructor that takes one iterable of iterables.
return list(chain.from_iterable(lists))
items.lesson: `chain(*its)` / `chain.from_iterable(its)` concatenate lazily, without building intermediate lists.
items.ts: lists.flatMap(l => [...l])

items.title: First n of an infinite stream
items.prompt: Write `first_n(iterable, n)` returning a list of the first `n` items. It must work on infinite iterators like `itertools.count()`.
hints: You can't slice a generator with [:n].
itertools.islice(iterable, n) is the lazy slice.
return list(islice(iterable, n))
items.lesson: `islice(it, stop)` or `islice(it, start, stop, step)` slices any iterator lazily — it only pulls the items it needs.
items.ts: const out = []; for (const x of it) { if (out.length >= n) break; out.push(x) }

items.title: Running totals and max
items.prompt:
Write `running(nums)` returning `(totals, maxes)`: the running sum and running max as lists.

`[3, 1, 4]` → `([3, 4, 8], [3, 3, 4])`
hints: itertools.accumulate yields running results; by default it adds.
accumulate(nums, max) uses max instead of +.
return list(accumulate(nums)), list(accumulate(nums, max))
items.lesson: `accumulate(xs)` = prefix sums; pass any 2-arg function (`max`, `operator.mul`) for other running values. Use `initial=0` to prepend a 0.
items.ts: let s = 0; nums.map(x => (s += x))

items.title: Pairs that sum to target
items.prompt: Write `pairs_to(nums, target)` returning every pair `(a, b)` (in input order, a before b) whose sum is `target`.
hints: itertools has a function for all unordered pairs (no repeats, no reversed duplicates).
combinations(nums, 2) yields (a, b) tuples with a earlier than b.
return [p for p in combinations(nums, 2) if sum(p) == target]
items.lesson: `combinations(xs, r)` = unordered picks (n choose r); `permutations(xs, r)` = ordered; `product(a, b)` = nested loops. All lazy.
items.ts: nums.flatMap((a, i) => nums.slice(i + 1).map(b => [a, b])).filter(([a, b]) => a + b === target)

items.title: All anagrams
items.prompt: Write `anagrams(word)` returning every distinct rearrangement of `word`, sorted.
hints: permutations(word) yields tuples of characters.
"".join(p) turns a tuple back into a string; a set removes duplicates.
return sorted({"".join(p) for p in permutations(word)})
items.lesson: `permutations` treats positions as distinct, so repeated letters produce duplicates — dedupe with a set comprehension.
items.ts: // no built-in; you'd write a recursive generator

items.title: Differences between neighbours
items.prompt: Write `diffs(nums)`: `[1, 4, 9, 16]` → `[3, 5, 7]` using `itertools.pairwise`.
hints: pairwise(xs) yields (xs[0], xs[1]), (xs[1], xs[2]), ...
Unpack each pair in the comprehension: for a, b in pairwise(nums).
return [b - a for a, b in pairwise(nums)]
items.lesson: `pairwise` (3.10+) replaces `zip(xs, xs[1:])` and works on any iterator, not just lists.
items.ts: nums.slice(1).map((b, i) => b - nums[i])
items.alternative:
def diffs(nums):
    return [b - a for a, b in zip(nums, nums[1:])]

items.title: Dataclass with a list field
items.prompt: Make `Cart` a dataclass with `owner: str` and `items: list[str]` defaulting to an empty list, plus `add(item)`. Two carts must not share items.
items.tests:
def test_independent():
    a, b = Cart("ann"), Cart("bo")
    a.add("apple")
    assert a.items == ["apple"], f"a.items is {a.items!r}"
    assert b.items == [], "b must not see a's items"
def test_repr_and_eq():
    assert Cart("x") == Cart("x", []), "dataclasses generate __eq__"
    assert repr(Cart("x")) == "Cart(owner='x', items=[])", f"repr was {Cart('x')!r}"
hints: @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields.
A mutable default needs field(default_factory=list) — `= []` is rejected.
items: list[str] = field(default_factory=list); def add(self, item): self.items.append(item)
items.lesson: `field(default_factory=list)` builds a fresh list per instance — the dataclass fix for the mutable-default-argument trap.
items.ts: class Cart { items: string[] = []; constructor(public owner: string) {} }

items.title: Immutable, hashable point
items.prompt: Make `Point(x, y)` a FROZEN dataclass so points can go in a set and assignment raises an error. Add `moved(dx, dy)` returning a new Point.
hints: Pass an option to the decorator: @dataclass(...).
@dataclass(frozen=True) makes fields read-only and generates __hash__.
def moved(self, dx, dy): return Point(self.x + dx, self.y + dy)
items.lesson: `frozen=True` = immutable + hashable, so instances work as dict keys and set members. Use `dataclasses.replace(p, x=5)` to copy with changes.
items.ts: type Point = Readonly<{ x: number; y: number }>  // but no value-equality in a Set

items.title: Sortable versions
items.prompt: Make `Version(major, minor, patch)` a dataclass that supports `<`, `sorted()` and `max()` by (major, minor, patch).
hints: The dataclass decorator can generate comparison methods too.
@dataclass(order=True) compares instances like tuples of their fields, in declaration order.
@dataclass(order=True) class Version: major: int; minor: int; patch: int
items.lesson: `order=True` adds `<, <=, >, >=` comparing fields as a tuple in declaration order. Put the sort key fields first (or use `field(compare=False)` to skip one).
items.ts: versions.sort((a, b) => a.major - b.major || a.minor - b.minor || a.patch - b.patch)

items.title: Plain class with __repr__ and __eq__
items.prompt: Without dataclasses, write `Money(amount, currency)` so that `repr(Money(5, 'USD'))` is `"Money(5, 'USD')"` and equal amounts+currencies compare equal.
hints: __init__(self, ...) stores attributes on self. __repr__ returns a string; use !r to get quotes.
__eq__(self, other): return NotImplemented if other isn't a Money, else compare the fields.
def __eq__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, Money): return NotImplemented; return (self.amount, self.currency) == (other.amount, other.currency)
items.lesson: `self` is explicit. `f"{x!r}"` uses repr (adds quotes to strings). Return `NotImplemented` from `__eq__` for foreign types so Python can try the other side.
items.ts: class Money { constructor(public amount: number, public currency: string) {} toString() {...} }

items.title: Computed property with a setter
items.prompt: Write `Temperature(celsius)` with a `fahrenheit` property (`c * 9 / 5 + 32`) that can also be SET (updating celsius).
hints: @property turns a method into a read-only attribute (no parentheses when used).
Add a setter with @fahrenheit.setter on a second method of the same name.
@fahrenheit.setter / def fahrenheit(self, f): self.celsius = (f - 32) * 5 / 9
items.lesson: Start with plain attributes; switch to `@property` later without changing callers. That's why Python doesn't write getters/setters up front.
items.ts: get fahrenheit() { return this.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 }  set fahrenheit(f) { ... }

items.title: Type-hinted higher-order function
items.prompt: Write `apply_n(f, x, n)` that applies `f` to `x` n times. Annotate it: `f` takes an int and returns an int, `x` and `n` are ints, and it returns an int.
hints: Annotations go after a colon for params and after -> for the return type.
Callable[[int], int] means 'takes one int, returns int'. Import Callable from collections.abc (or typing).
def apply_n(f: Callable[[int], int], x: int, n: int) -> int:
items.lesson: Hints are not enforced at runtime — they're for readers and checkers (mypy/pyright). `Callable[[Arg1, Arg2], Ret]` mirrors TS `(a: Arg1, b: Arg2) => Ret`.
items.ts: function applyN(f: (v: number) => number, x: number, n: number): number

items.title: Optional return type
items.prompt: Write `find_user(users, name)`: `users` is a `dict[str, int]` (name → age). Return the age or `None`. Annotate params and return (`Optional[int]` or `int | None`).
hints: dict.get already returns None for a missing key.
Write the hints inline: users: dict[str, int], name: str, -> Optional[int].
def find_user(users: dict[str, int], name: str) -> Optional[int]: return users.get(name)
items.lesson: Built-in generics work directly as hints: `list[int]`, `dict[str, int]`, `tuple[int, ...]`. `Optional[X]` == `X | None` (3.10+ syntax).
items.ts: function findUser(users: Record<string, number>, name: string): number | undefined

items.title: Write then read a file
items.prompt: Write `save_lines(path, items)` (one item per line) and `load_lines(path)` (returns the lines without newlines). Use `with open(...)`.
items.tests:
import os, tempfile
def test_roundtrip():
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        p = os.path.join(d, "notes.txt")
        save_lines(p, ["alpha", "beta"])
        with open(p) as f:
            raw = f.read()
        assert raw == "alpha\nbeta\n", f"file content was {raw!r}"
        assert load_lines(p) == ["alpha", "beta"], f"load_lines gave {load_lines(p)!r}"
hints: open(path, "w") to write, open(path) to read; `with` closes the file for you.
Write each item followed by "\n". Reading: f.read().splitlines() drops the newlines.
with open(path, "w") as f: for x in items: f.write(x + "\n")  …  with open(path) as f: return f.read().splitlines()
items.lesson: Always `with open(...) as f:` — it closes the file even on errors. Pass `encoding="utf-8"`. `splitlines()` strips the line endings for you.
items.ts:
fs.writeFileSync(path, items.join('
') + '
'); fs.readFileSync(path, 'utf8').split('
')

items.title: Count non-blank lines in a file object
items.prompt: Write `count_nonblank(f)` where `f` is any open text file (tests pass an `io.StringIO`). Iterate it line by line.
hints: Iterating a file yields one line at a time (with its trailing newline).
line.strip() is falsy for blank and whitespace-only lines.
return sum(1 for line in f if line.strip())
items.solution:
def count_nonblank(f):
    return sum(1 for line in f if line.strip())
items.lesson: Write functions that take a file OBJECT, not a path — then tests can pass `io.StringIO(...)` and nothing touches disk. `for line in f` streams the file.
items.ts: text.split('\n').filter(l => l.trim()).length

items.title: Pretty, stable JSON
items.prompt: Write `pretty(obj)` returning JSON with 2-space indentation and keys sorted alphabetically.
hints: json.dumps turns Python objects into a JSON string; keyword options control the layout.
indent=2 for indentation, sort_keys=True for stable key order.
return json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
items.lesson: `dumps`/`loads` work with strings; `dump`/`load` with files. `sort_keys=True` makes output diff-friendly.

items.title: Serialize dates with default=
items.prompt: Write `to_json(obj)` so that `datetime.date` values become ISO strings: `{'d': date(2024, 1, 2)}` → `'{"d": "2024-01-02"}'`.
hints: json.dumps raises TypeError for types it doesn't know — unless you give it a fallback.

items.lesson: `default=fn` is called only for unknown types. Raise TypeError for anything you don't handle, so real bugs still surface. (`default=str` is the quick-and-dirty version.)

items.title: Max-heap that returns the wrong sign
items.code:
import heapq

def largest_first(nums):
    h = [-n for n in nums]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    out = []
    while h:
        out.append(heapq.heappop(h))
    return out
items.fixed:
import heapq

def largest_first(nums):
    h = [-n for n in nums]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    out = []
    while h:
        out.append(-heapq.heappop(h))
    return out
items.tests:
def test_order():
    assert largest_first([3, 1, 2]) == [3, 2, 1], f"got {largest_first([3, 1, 2])!r}"
items.explanation: heapq is min-only, so the max-heap trick stores `-n`. You must negate again when popping, otherwise you return the negated values.

items.title: Grouping words by length
choices: Sort by the same key first: `groupby(sorted(words, key=len), key=len)`
items.explanation: groupby only groups adjacent items, so unsorted input yields the same key several times and later groups overwrite earlier ones. Sort by the grouping key first (or use defaultdict(list)).
